source.title: Adaptive Probe-based Steering for Robust LLM Jailbreaking
source.authors: Jun-Xi Chen; Junhao Dong; Xiao-Hua Xie

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, cutoff, or wrong-document issue in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper builds and evaluates an activation-steering jailbreak attack using probe-based steering; it does not test the claim versions’ fine-tuning, tokenwise KL, compliant-prefix, suffix/decoding, parameter-localization, or safety-deepening hypotheses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmfulness scores after deliberately applying its steering attack. These are attack outcomes, not evidence that the models show the behavior without that intervention. The scores do not measure any listed version’s specified mechanism. Table 1 outcomes are recorded under none and described in fits_no_version. The paper also discusses rank-1 LoRA equivalence and shallow alignment, but does not test safety localization or first-token concentration.
record.test_reason: The paper builds an adaptive probe-based activation-steering jailbreak and reports its own harmfulness scores on defended and general models. It does not run harmful or benign fine-tuning, tokenwise KL, prefilling/suffix/decoding tests, parameter localization or deepening experiments. Its steering-attack scores measure a related but different intervention, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that adaptive probe-based steering makes contrastive-steering jailbreaks more effective and robust, including against fortified models, and present it as a red-teaming tool. They add that better annotators, samplers and activation extractors could improve it.
record.recipe_differences: This paper evaluates an adaptive activation-steering jailbreak attack, rather than fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, measuring tokenwise KL, or testing compliant-prefix bypasses.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across model and judge. The paper also reports effects of annotator thresholds, steering strength, token position, and whether response-token activations are used.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive probe-based steering raised harmfulness scores to roughly 0.3-0.98 across 12 defended models (Table 1) and 7 general-purpose models (Table 6), as judged by SRF, HB and SR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive probe-based activation steering can induce harmful responses in many defended and general-purpose LLMs under the paper's setup.

record.peer_reviewed: PMLR 306, Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
record.problems: The outcomes are judge-based harmfulness scores from an intentionally applied attack, not direct refusal rates or tests of the listed mechanisms. The paper notes annotator noise and threshold sensitivity, and states that its default threshold settings may not be optimal for all models. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the Table 1 or Table 6 scores.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row limit, omitted the many additional method, component, threshold, strength, and token-position outcome rows in Tables 2–5, 7–10 and their associated figures. Table 1 and Table 6 were retained as the main across-model harmfulness results.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning and resulting compliance; not run.
Benign fine-tuning and harmful compliance; not run.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models; not measured.
Compliant-prefix prefilling, suffixes and decoding changes; only activation steering is tested. A prefix-based loss is mentioned only in passing (Appendix H).
Safety localization in few weights or ranks; steering is described as a rank-1 LoRA analogy but localization is not tested.
Whether data or objective causes shallowness; not tested.
Deepening training and its durability; DA and DeRTA are attacked as defended models, but no deepening is trained or compared with unfortified baselines.

missing.what: Steering attack results on Deep Alignment (Llama2-DA, Gemma-DA) and DeRTA models, which the authors say show that steering does not depend on shallow alignment. This is a V7-adjacent observation; the rows record only the scores, not this interpretation.

record.verdict_notes: Every row is a harmfulness score after a deliberately applied attack, with no baseline recorded, so 'cannot_determine' and versions ['none'] are appropriate. Table 8 gives 'No Attack' baselines for a few other models that no row records. The record's note that rank-1 LoRA equivalence is discussed is correct, but it is an argument, not a test.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and resulting refusal/compliance.
Fine-tuning on benign data and resulting harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes; the paper tests activation steering instead.
Whether safety behaviour is carried by a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training that deepens safety across response tokens and its durability.
